title: ARTICLE ARCHIVE Education What Are We Measuring Rethinking Mock Exams
author: Solomons, Mark
summary: Solomons describes how a colleague's review of their Year 10 mock examination window led to a fundamental redesign -- fewer papers, capped timing -- after asking: what is this window of testing actually for? Drawing on testing-effect literature, he distinguishes low-stakes frequent retrieval (which builds memory) from high-stakes compressed exam replication (which measures coping under pressure more than mastery). Using Daisy Christodoulou's marathon analogy: you do not train for a marathon by running marathons in training. The central problem with a compressed Year 10 mock season is construct validity -- grades reflect fatigue, sleep management, and stress tolerance as much as curriculum knowledge. Domain-coverage problems further blur the signal: midway through a two-year course, unlearned content makes underperformance uninterpretable. The redesigned model preserves exam-style structure while reducing load, producing cleaner data and calmer students. The broader argument: assessment must be designed around its intended purpose, not around surface resemblance to the final exam.
points: - The testing effect supports low-stakes frequent retrieval for memory consolidation, but high-stakes compressed mock seasons measure stress tolerance and stamina rather than curriculum mastery -- the construct shifts. - Construct validity is the central problem: ten full papers in two weeks produces data that reflects coping under artificial compression, not a clean measure of what students know. - Daisy Christodoulou's marathon analogy is precise: placing students under high-stakes exam conditions before the knowledge base and conditioning that would allow genuine performance is secure mistakes rehearsal for training. - Domain-coverage problems further blur mid-course data: unlearned content on full past papers makes it impossible to attribute underperformance cleanly to a knowledge gap versus premature exposure. - Assessment design should follow from assessment purpose, not from surface resemblance to the final exam -- a diagnostic checkpoint requires a different design than a performance simulation.
quotes: The Year 10 examination window is not primarily about generating grades. Its value is in producing information that improves learning. It should function as a diagnostic mid-course checkpoint: generating valid, reliable and actionable data that helps departments identify strengths and gaps.

The testing effect is one of the most replicated findings in cognitive science. Retrieval strengthens memory, and when students are required to pull knowledge from long-term memory, learning improves. Frequent, low-stakes retrieval helps information stick, strengthens recall pathways and makes forgetting less likely.

Daisy Christodoulou draws on a memorable analogy in Making Good Progress: you do not train for a marathon by running a marathon every training session. The full distance is the test of preparation, not the method of building it. The same logic applies in classrooms.
If a Year 10 student sits multiple two-hour papers across many subjects within a two-week window, the data does not purely reflect curriculum mastery. It reflects coping under artificial compression.

Wellbeing is not a second order consideration here. Performance science shows that acute stress can sharpen attention in short bursts. Sustained stress across multiple high-demand tasks does not: it degrades working memory, disrupts sleep and erodes emotional control.

By reducing the overall load, they produce cleaner data, protect student wellbeing and give departments something they can genuinely act on, rather than a dataset distorted by fatigue and artificial compression.
Assessment should strengthen memory, clarify gaps and guide teaching. A tighter, more deliberate model produces better data, stronger learning and calmer students.
